segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At that time Herod the tetrarch heard the report about Jesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he said to his servants,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This is John the Baptist. He has been raised from the dead, and that is why these powers are at work in him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Herod had seized John, bound him, and put him away in prison on account of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because John had been telling him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is not lawful for you to have her.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Though he wanted to kill him, he was afraid of the crowd, because they held him to be a prophet.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when Herod’s birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced in front of the company and pleased Herod,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she asked.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Prompted by her mother, she said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Give me here, on a platter, the head of John the Baptist.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The king was grieved, but because of his oaths and his dinner guests he ordered it to be given,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he sent and had John beheaded in the prison.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His disciples came, took away the corpse, and buried him; then they went and told Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there by boat to a deserted place by himself. But the crowds heard of it and followed him on foot from the towns.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he came ashore he saw a large crowd, and he was moved with compassion for them and healed their sick.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When evening came, the disciples approached him and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This is a deserted place, and the hour is already late. Send the crowds away, so that they can go into the villages and buy themselves food.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “They do not need to go away. You give them something to eat.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have nothing here except five loaves and two fish.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Bring them here to me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he ordered the crowds to recline on the grass. Taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing; then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They all ate and were satisfied, and they picked up what was left over of the broken pieces—twelve baskets full.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat and go ahead of him to the other side, while he sent the crowds away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After sending the crowds away, he went up the mountain by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The boat was already a long way from the land, battered by the waves, for the wind was against it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is a ghost!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they cried out in fear.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But at once Jesus spoke to them:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Take courage; it is I. Do not be afraid.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Come.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Peter got down out of the boat, walked on the water, and came toward Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when he saw the strong wind, he became afraid, and beginning to sink he cried out,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, save me!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when they got into the boat, the wind died down.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those in the boat worshiped him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Truly you are the Son of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The men of that place recognized him and sent word throughout that whole surrounding region, and people brought to him all who were sick,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they begged him to let them just touch the tassel of his cloak; and all who touched it were made completely well.

notes.note: This is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea under Rome. “Tetrarch” was the title of a dependent ruler ranking below a king. Matthew calls him “the king” in verse 9, which reflects popular usage and not his official rank.

The Greek word is the ordinary word for power. In the plural it often means miracles, which is how the KJV takes it here (“mighty works do shew forth themselves in him”). Because these are said to be “at work in him,” most modern versions understand forces operating through Jesus rather than the deeds themselves, and the translation follows that reading.

notes.phrase: It is not lawful for you to have her
notes.note: Herodias had left her first husband, Antipas’s half-brother, to marry Antipas. The Law of Moses forbade a man to marry his brother’s wife while the brother was alive (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). The Greek verb tense indicates that John said this repeatedly.

The Greek verb has no stated object, so it can be read as blessing the food or as blessing God. In Jewish practice the prayer before a meal blessed God for the food, and that is the more likely sense here. “Said a blessing” leaves the object open as the Greek does.

notes.traditional: many furlongs / in the midst of the sea
notes.note: The Greek says “many stadia”; a stadion was about 185 meters or 600 feet, so the boat was well out on the lake. Many manuscripts read instead “in the middle of the sea,” as in Mark 6:47, and the KJV follows that reading.

notes.phrase: the fourth watch of the night
notes.note: The Roman system divided the night into four watches. The fourth was the last, running from roughly three to six in the morning, so the disciples had been struggling against the wind for most of the night.

The Greek is literally “I am,” the normal way to say “It’s me.” The same words are also God’s self-identification in the Greek Old Testament (for example Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 43:10). Many scholars think Matthew intends that echo here, in a scene where Jesus walks on the sea and is then worshiped; others take it as simple self-identification.
A few important early manuscripts lack the word “strong” and read simply “when he saw the wind.” Editors are divided on whether the word is original, but the sense is little affected.

The Greek has no definite article and could be rendered “God’s Son” or, less probably, “a son of God.” Greek often leaves out the article before a noun in this position, and Matthew’s later use of the title (16:16; 27:54) supports the definite sense adopted here and in most translations.

The Greek word can mean the edge of a garment. It is also the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the tassels that Israelite men were commanded to wear on the corners of their cloaks as a reminder of God’s commandments (Numbers 15:38–39). Matthew uses it in that sense at 23:5, and it most likely means the same here. Most translations have “fringe” or “hem.”

candidates.reason: Recurs across the Synoptics of Jesus and in parables; versions vary between “had compassion,” “felt pity,” and “was moved with compassion,” and readers should see one rendering.
A distinctive address in Matthew and Luke that needs one fixed English form, and that should be coordinated with the register’s treatment of πίστις.
Occurs in Matthew 9:20; 14:36; 23:5 and the parallels in Mark and Luke; “hem,” “fringe,” and “tassel” are all in use, and the choice should be the same everywhere.
A unit of distance in the Gospels and Revelation; a single policy is needed on whether to keep “stadia,” convert to modern units, or paraphrase.
Contrasted with σπυρίς in the two feeding accounts and in Matthew 16:9–10, so the two basket words need distinct, consistent renderings across the Gospels.
